speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONSENT BY MEMBER FOR BATTLE RIVER TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43-RULING BY MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Yesterday when the hon. member for Battle River proposed a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 the Chair declined to put the motion as proposed and undertook to study the circumstances and make a ruling. After careful consideration it seems to me that very little can be added to my comments as recorded at pages 9073 and 9074 of yesterday's debates.
I suggest to the House that the purpose of Standing Order 43 was never intended to permit an hon. member to launch a unilateral debate. It is my view that it is not in accord with the practices and proprieties of this House to use the Standing Order for such purposes when in effect it is intended only to suspend the notice requirement for a motion. It is my judgment that a member, when proposing a motion under Standing Order 43, should restrict his comments to the necessity or desirability of suspending the notice provision for a motion. It seems to me that any enlargement of that prior condition would end inevitably in great difficulty as the same Standing Order could be used from both sides of the House for the purpose of questioning the conduct of any or every member of the House.
As hon. members know, the House has developed well established and recognized procedures for the purpose of discussing the conduct of ministers and of members of the House. It is a prime duty of the Chair to safeguard the interests of all hon. members. Under the circumstances I cannot ask the House whether the hon. member for Battle River has the unanimous consent of the House to propose the motion to which he alluded yesterday.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, because of the questions that have been raised on this matter in the House, I am pleased to announce that the Agricultural Products Board has invited tenders for a total of 3,600,000 pounds of eviscerated turkey. The purchase price ranges between 33 cents and 40 cents per pound. Since these birds must be of current kill it is anticipated that the purchase will have a favourable impact on producer returns immediately.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for the announcement he has made about the government's purchase of turkeys. I hope it will bring about a slight rise in price to the producers. There may be some difficulty because the Agricultural Products Board has stipulated that the turkeys have to be fresh killed rather than frozen even though there is an abundance of frozen turkeys in storage. A good deal of the product has gone to market and those who kill fresh turkeys have regular customers for whom they have to keep turkeys available. This may make it difficult for the program to be of as much help as it would have been if it had been announced sooner and if frozen turkeys had been included. However, for what has been done we are thankful and we hope it will be helpful.

The House resumed, from Wednesday, October 27, consideration in committee of Bill C-259, to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that act-Mr. Benson-Mr. Honey in the chair.
On clause 1-section 4: Income or loss from a source or from sources in a place.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. When the committee rose last evening, section 4 was before the committee. It had been agreed to include sections 5, 6, 7 and 8 with section 4 for the purposes of discussion. Shall section 4 carry?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some brief comments, particularly upon subsection (6) of section 6, which is related to subsections 7 and 8 immediately following. This matter was raised yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. As hon. members of the committee will note if they look at this part, this provision is a modification of paragraph 5(2) of the present act.
My initial comment on this matter must be that it is better to do something late than never. I rise to support this particular proposal in the bill because it is something I have been seeking to have included in the Income Tax Act for over 15 years. In 1956, the Liberal minister of finance, Hon. Walter Harris, indicated to me after I had been raising this matter for two or three sessions that, in his view, there was a discrimination in this regard in the Income Tax Act as it then stood and as it still stands after having been modified. The act discriminated against those who maintain a domestic establishment in one place and, as a result of their employment, have to leave home, pay room and board elsewhere as well as travelling expenses in order to undertake their particular kind of work. Our attempts to convince the government that the law in this regard discriminated against a group of workers have been long and arduous.
The particular groups of workers in my area, and in British Columbia generally, who have been most affected by this discrimination are the loggers. Over a period, three of their organizations have made many submissions on this subject to the government. Those submissions were well reasoned and well documented. I am sure that those organizations welcome the change that is being brought forward because, at long last, they will be treated with the same degree of equity as other segments in the work force of our society have been treated in connection with expense allowances. I am thinking in particular of those who may have been working in a managerial capacity.
Recently I had the opportunity to speak to a union convention in Vancouver. A large number of loggers were there as delegates. I told them that this proposal was in the Income Tax Act after 15 years of argument on this subject, that I had read the section rather carefully and that, so far as I could see, the wording of the law covered
October 28, 1971

the point adequately. I reminded them, and I should like to remind hon. members of the committee and the ministers concerned, in particular the Minister of National Revenue, that from time to time that minister's department issue what we refer to as information bulletins. These bulletins often indicate what the law means for practical purposes. I told them, as I now say to members of the committee, that I hope the information bulletins put out by the Department of National Revenue will place a proper and reasonable interpretation upon the application of this proposed section of the Income Tax Act so that it will provide the kind of situation which, from my reading of the proposed clause, it is intended to provide for these taxpayers.
I hope there will be no battles as the result of an interpretation being placed on that section which is so narrow and restrictive as to make the section practically worthless. That is something that those of us who are concerned about the matter will be watching, and if the subsection is not construed to mean what its language in my opinion clearly intends, there will, of course, be some battles in and out of the chamber on that subject.
I think I have made it clear that when the government does take a step which I consider to be right and proper, as one who sits on the opposition side of the House, I am quite happy to commend the government for its action. Perhaps my appreciation may be all the more heartfelt because of the fact it has taken 15 years for me to get to the point where I can stand in this chamber and say the words I am saying today. I hope the minister will recognize the fact that we are trying to take a fair look at his bill. We will praise it when praise is merited. However, we will differ from it where we feel it is not working in the best interests of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am going to deal with section 7. This is the section that treats shares that are given to employees during the year as income. In view of the situation in which we in Canada are going to find ourselves, I am not so sure I fully support this view. A little while ago I might have, but it seems that in the next few months, year or two years, we are going to be looking for Canadian shareholders. We will be trying to entice them to hold shares, preferably in the plants and concerns in which they are employed. Some incentive has to be given to them. If these shares are treated as income during the current year, that is not exactly an incentive.
I say to the Minister of Finance that we are also going to be faced with the problem of productivity. I have stated on many occasions that it is always very bad when we have labour-management problems and when we have low productivity on the part of Canadian workmen. The question always arises, how can we induce Canadians to produce more? I suggest that one of the best ways is to give them a piece of the action. In other words, we should make it enticing and advantageous for workmen, employees, junior executives and senior executives to own shares in the plants and concerns in which they are employed. I hope that over a period of time labour-management negotiations will not be based on a wage differential or, for example, the desire for an extra two or three days. I hope that over a period of time negotiations will be
Income Tax Act
based on organized labour requiring more shares of the company.
One of the great problems of our economy is that we do not have enough shareholders. I dare say if we investigated the members in this House, a handful might be owners of shares in Canadian corporations. Of that handful, the chances are that most of them have acquired shares in penny stocks and mining shares. If some elevator operator says it is a good idea to buy Moose Pasture No. 1, Canadians will immediately go out and buy it. However, as far as holding investments from a long range point of view, Canadians do not hold shares. The share holdings are restricted to very small groups.
One of our problems of distribution of dividends is that there are not enough people to whom we can distribute them. In other words, there is not a broad spectrum of shareholders. Instead of taxing shares in companies in which the taxpayers are employed on a full-time basis, it would be preferable to tax them on a 50 per cent basis. An inducement such as that would be more likely to have the effect that the employees would own a big chunk of the business in which they are employed. In order to get more dividends and also the capital gains, which are also included in the latter part of this bill, there would be an inducement to be productive.
If the minister investigates the companies in Canada which now have or have had a share distribution plan, he will find that these are the companies which are more productive. They have less problems with management because everyone is in on the action. To start out immediately under this new bill and say that if you happen to get shares in your company, they will be treated as income for the current year will be no inducement to employees to hold shares. I seriously recommend that the minister review his thoughts on this section. Instead of the full value of the shares presumed to be income, that provision should be amended to read 50 per cent of the value of the shares.

I wonder if I might direct a question to the parliamentary secretary, since there are going to be further observations about the matter as we go along. Under sections 109 and 110, I raised the point of the rationale for establishing age 21 as the age of majority. Certain provinces have now made 18 the legal age of majority. We understand that the province of Quebec proposes to introduce legislation in the very near future to the same effect. Nearly 80 per cent of young Canadians will be subject to a legal age of majority of 18, yet this income tax bill treats the division as age 21. I would like a clear understanding from the Department of Finance on this whole question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, for clarification, may I reply? I think the hon. member will appreciate that there was some confusion when he was starting his remarks. Is the member referring to the same item he raised the other day in connection with the exemption being extended to a child resident in his parents' home until age 21?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, that is so. That is one of them. I did not hear any explanation or answer to my question. I know this is going to arise in relation to paragraph 63, child care expenses, where the

October 28, 1971
Income Tax Act
relative who is disqualified is under the age of 21. We are getting this continued use of the age 21 throughout the piece. I am giving the parliamentary secretary due notice.
I raised this matter the other day and I am again raising it. I am sure some of my colleagues and possibly some of the members opposite will raise the point again in the future. I think this matter should be looked at. There may be a valid reason why the present status should be left as is, but I fail to see it at the present time.
I now wish to turn to section 4 (4) which appears at the foot of page 4.1 am wondering whether this is one of those sections which have been thrown in to grant extraordinary discretionary powers of judgment to the minister. When I was discussing this matter at an earlier stage I indicated that, somehow, it always appears that the advantage shall lie with the Crown. Never is there equity on behalf of the taxpayer or never is the situation even as between the two, even though the law is patently unfair. It was always interpreted in such a way that the Crown cannot lose. I am wondering whether this is one of those sections. In any event I invite the parliamentary secretary or the minister to give us in reasonable terms, in clear language, an explanation of what is meant by this subsection. I read:
p.tn.)
Unless a contrary intention is evident, no provision of this Part shall be read or construed to require the inclusion or to permit the deduction, in computing the income of a taxpayer for a taxation year or his income or loss for a taxation year from a particular source or from sources in a particular place, of any amount to the extent that that amount has been included or deducted, as the case may be, in computing such income or loss under, in accordance with or by virtue of any other provision of this Part.
I am sorry, but my legal training and experience to date have not enabled me to translate into straightforward language what the drafters of the legislation meant by this particular paragraph. It is a new paragraph, and therefore it has not been the subject of any previous departmental rulings or of interpretation by tax consultants. Sub-paragraph (2) is also a new provision but it does not appear to give us much difficulty. We have seen many instances of tax authorities saying that this bill, using new terms, has unfortunately led to an entirely new family of language which is thoroughly unfamiliar to the profession and even less familiar to a taxpayer. There is no way of arriving at a ruling.
I want to go back to a point I made on second reading. The efficacy of a tax statute and the justice of a tax statute depend upon the ability of the person who has to pay the tax to understand it. We are now being led into an even greater maze of uncertainty all the way along. I cannot understand how government members, particularly, can claim in this House that they are engaging in tax reform when they are asking us to inflict upon the country an income tax act even less comprehensible than the existing one. This does not make sense. The charge of obscurity has been a common charge, even taking into account the fact that lack of familiarity with new sections leads to difficulty and that some people throw up their hands and say the changes must be bad because they cannot be understood. But even those whose experience has given them considerable practice in the interpretation
(Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West).]
of these subsections cannot say how this legislation will work out.
This is illustrated by the point I am trying to make in connection with section (4) subsection (iv): there are many businesses today whose business operations in 1971 will be subject to law in 1972. That law will be retroactive. They cannot understand it now, and as a matter of fact the transactions into which they enter in 1971 will be subject to a law which they did not even know existed, because the bill had not been published. This is an example of what I call the latent injustice which appears in the bill. Hon. members may be puzzled as to what I am saying, but in actual fact this is so. In due course we shall come to some sections which will show that there are retroactive features in this bill, in particular dealing with business, covering transactions which occurred maybe six months before this bill had even been published. This is an example of the injustice which occurs as a result of imprecise language or muddled language and sections whic|j are very difficult to interpret.
I should like to turn to section 6, because there we are dealing with certain items which must be included in the income of an individual. A lot of the wording is carried forward from the existing act. I do not think we have any problems with 6(l)(a) or with 6(l)(b) which, again, is a carry-forward. Then, we come to something which is new, namely, 6(l)(e) dealing with the stand-by charge for automobiles. This will certainly lead to litigation. There are no two ways about it. The results are likely to be most unfair. The automobile referred to is to be made available for personal use or otherwise. Now, if the main purpose of the automobile is for business, does the section apply? Or is it caught by, maybe, a 5 per cent or 10 per cent segment that is for personal use? The phrase in parenthesis appearing at line 25 does not assist us-
"Exclusive" may be read as meaning for the benefit of that one employee as opposed to several employees rather than referring to an exclusive type of use.
These are the difficulties which arise when we say "for his exclusive personal use or otherwise". Does it mean it is exclusive personal use or does it cover other circumstances? If an employee has to share an automobile with others, why should he be hit for a charge? This is the nature of the imprecise language which is used.
Then, we come to Section 6(2). The leasing formula and the capital formula could result in different contributions to an employee depending on the type of arrangement the employer makes. The employee's benefit is constant. But why would it not have been better to use a percentage based on the cost of the car? Whether the car is leased or owned, what is the difference? The question is, what is it that we are taxing? It is the value to an employee of an automobile that has been given to him for his personal use, not for his business use but his personal use. Therefore, why go into a whole rigmarole as to whether the car is leased by the firm or owned by the firm? What effect has that on the nature of the tax? Why does the tax department concern itself with that consideration? All that is being done is the allocation to the employee for his personal use of a car worth so many dollars. That an employee can understand, and that I can understand; indeed, I think just about anybody can understand it. Instead of that, we are taken down the garden path by a
October 28, 1971

long formula. I do not think that this provision helps this statute.
Section 6(l)(f) deals with employment insurance benefits, and here again I think an injustice is done. The employee is charged with the benefits if the employer makes a contribution. In such case the benefit received is taxed as a deduction for the dollar value of the premiums paid by the employee. If the employee pays all of the contributions then the benefits are not taxable; but should his employer pay just $1, then all of the benefits less the employee's portion of the premiums are chargeable. I cannot see the logic of this. Would it not be more consistent to base the benefit of the employee on that portion that is paid? If his employer pays half the premiums, then why not charge half of the benefits to the employee? If the employer pays 10 per cent, then the employee should only be charged with 10 per cent of the benefits. I think that is the only way.
I should like to pass on now to section 6(8). Here again I should like to reiterate the arguments made by a number of my colleagues. Frankly, I cannot see in this day and age why we are establishing that in business terms a wife is to be regarded separately from her husband, particularly in cases where a husband and wife are working together. Why cannot a distinction be made between them?
I would say this provision is an unnecessary exercise. It is a shame to force the husband to incorporate his business. He owns all the shares, though his solicitor can hold one qualifying share in order to make it a private company. His wife can work as a secretary or clerk and receive pay, but her income is treated separately and the parties are taxed as two individuals. In many cases in order to do this work the wife has to hire assistance to take care of her children, which would qualify her for child care benefits. However, under the act we consistently deny this distinction between husband and wife. Not only is the salary paid to the wife not considered as an expense of the business, but she will not be able to qualify under the child care benefit provision of the act.
Even further than that, suppose the husband is in partnership with one or more individuals. Let us take the case of two or three doctors and a dentist who are in partnership in a small country town. In order to operate their office efficiently the wife of one of them, who may be a trained nurse, acts as a nursing assistant or as nurse-receptionist at their clinic. In order to do so, however, she has to hire someone to look after her children. At the present time, because her husband is a member of a partnership her salary is not deductible as an expense of the partnership. Even though this is a legitimate expenditure that is normal for such a business, just because she happens to be the wife of one of the partners her salary is not regarded as a business expense. In addition to that, section 63 denies this wife who is acting as a receptionist to the doctors and dentist, child care allowance.
If the parliamentary secretary would rather I got away from the professions, take the case of the trucking firm, the plastering firm or two or three plumbers who work together. They do not incorporate their business and have good reason not to do so. As my colleague from Lambton-Kent pointed out, because of credit restrictions or other
Income Tax Act
conditions banks may prefer them not to incorporate. Nevertheless, someone has to keep the books and answer the telephone on a half day basis.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, and I do so only to advise him and the committee that his time has expired.
Continue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee give unanimous consent?
Mr. Chairman, if the parliamentary secretary wishes to speak, let him do so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We seem to be building up a good sized inventory of inquiries and comments, so probably I should take an opportunity to deal with at least some of these.
The question which the hon. member for Edmonton West just raised was brought to us in terms of the "Momma and Poppa corner store" by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants and a number of other speakers during consideration of sections 4 to 8 of the bill. The provision they are actually complaining about is contained in section 74(4).
Section 6(8).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No, to be perfectly clear, section 6(8) contains the saving provision which makes certain that people who receive that kind of income, which is not deductible by the husband, do not have to include it in their income. To make it very clear, they are not taxed on the payments their spouse would not be able to deduct from his income. Strictly speaking, the problem complained about arises in section 74, and with respect I would suggest that is the place to deal with the point. The point has been noted and we certainly will deal with it at that time.
The question of exclusive use of an automobile in section 6(l)(e) has been raised by a number of speakers. The word "exclusive" there is designed to make sure that the benefit is taxable in the hands of the taxpayer, whether the vehicle is for his exclusive personal use or for mixed business and personal use, and it goes back to the root definition of income being the sum total of benefits which the taxpayer obtains from his employment.
The matter of salary continuation insurance or income maintenance plans referred to in section 6(l)(f) has also been raised on numerous occasions. Some members have suggested that an employee should be able to deduct his premiums, or a portion of the benefits attributable to that part of the premium paid by the employee should not be taxable. The bill before the House does provide that an employee may not deduct his premiums paid to a plan each year, but when a benefit is received the employee will be able to deduct from the benefit all premiums paid since 1967, not previously deducted. In other words, he will be allowed his own contributions free of tax before any amount is added to his income. Again, we get back to the root concept of a man's income being the sum total of benefits he receives from employment.

October 28, 1971
Income Tax Act
The matter of strike pay was raised in an inquiry by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants. The bill does not provide for taxation on strike pay in the hands of the recipient. The question of employee stock options has been raised by the hon. member as well as by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services and one or two others. Here again, there is no significant change in this bill from the law as it exists. Members, raising this point, have taken exception to a change in the present Income Tax Act which was made a couple of years ago, which did remove some exceptionally favourable treatment that was accorded taxpayers in a position to receive stock option plans. This is a valid point and it is an important point but there is no change proposed in this bill from the existing law.
The matter of expenses of workmen employed away from home was welcomed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as the result of long effort by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, which has finally been rewarded. I am happy to note that welcome and the congratulations from that side in respect of this action. Certainly I must say I regard it as a very significant step forward.
The question of union dues was also raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, with reference to section 8(l)(i). The hon. member expressed the assumption that special assessments might be included for deduction of union dues. This section is not changed at all from the previous law. There is no particular reason to think at this point that the Department of National Revenue will interpret this section of the bill any differently from the way in which it interprets the identical section in the existing Income Tax Act. Officials of the Department of National Revenue have advised me that annual membership dues to a union are deductible even though part of the dues may be earmarked for a strike fund, but a special levy that is imposed because of a particular event, which represents more of a one shot thing rather than a year after year or annual payment, is not deductible. Section 8(5)(c) is relevant to this and I should call it to the hon. member's attention. This paragraph provides that annual dues are not deductible under section 8 when they are paid for any purpose not directly related to the operating expenses of the trade union to which they were paid. An example has been cited in which a portion of the annual dues have been earmarked to build up a fund to help finance housing for members of the union, or something like that, and that might not be deductible. As I said before, this particular section is unchanged from the existing Income Tax Act.
The matter of employment expenses and allowances has been noted by a number of members, and this is under section 8(1) (a) (i). This debate has been going on since the white paper was tabled with its proposals which are essentially carried forward in this bill unchanged, and no doubt was carried on well before that when many people saw a measure of inequity in that a salary or wage earner is not allowed to deduct many of the expenses incurred in earning income whereas the proprietor frequently can, and whereas an executive often has those expenses paid for him by his employer, which in turn are deductible by the employees. It has been suggested that the $150 ceiling be changed to a tax credit or that it be

increased in some way. The law permits a deduction for a substantial number of specific expenses such as the union dues I have just mentioned, and other expenses of employees which are described in section 8 and various subsections, including expenses for meals and lodging incurred by employees who have to travel in the course of their employment, legal expenses incurred in collecting salaries and wages, and so on. This bill does introduce in the 3 per cent or $150 ceiling an employee expense allowance which is an important new deduction. The bill also introduces a new deduction in terms of unemployment insurance premiums. It also makes an important change in section 6(6), extending to all employees the right to exclude benefits in cash for kind received from an employer to cover the cost of travelling to or living at a distant work site. This was also the cause of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
The new general deduction is an attempt to provide a deduction for other expenses. The requests for deductions of a more general nature have been studied for many years by governments, but this is a very difficult problem. One of the main difficulties is finding a reasonable and fair stopping place, if a start were made to allow new deductions for amounts spent by an employee in connection with his employment.
In addition to tools used by garage mechanics there are tools used by other trades such as carpenters, painters, plumbers and radio repair men. Expenses for getting to and from work are regarded by many as expenses necessarily incurred to earn salaries or wages. In some cases special clothing is required. Some employees, such as teachers and clergymen, find they have to buy books, tape recorders and typewriters to perform their work. A case can be made that amounts spent on all these items and numerous other items should be deducted in computing income. But if such a list of deductions were allowed, there would be a very real problem in checking and controlling all the receipts involved, and the substantial loss of revenue that would result would have to be recovered eslewhere in higher rates of tax on the remaining taxable income or perhaps through other forms of taxation than income tax.
As I said, this 3 per cent deduction is an important step. Combined with the other deductions permitted to employees, such as moving expenses and so on that are new under this bill, the estimate of the revenue loss in this area is $285 million, the first year that the new system is in effect based on the 1970 income tax payments. This is the largest single income reduction item in the package, taking into account that the rate schedules plus the exemptions should be treated as a package. So, I suggest that it is a great step forward. It is one that I am sure the government will watch with interest to see how it works. I hope we will find some way of creating more equity, but I commend it to hon. members as a very important new approach in the Canadian tax law.
The question of meals claimed away from home under section 8 (g) was raised by the hon. member for Portneuf and also the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. The problem that they seem to be raising is not related to any provision in the bill itself, but to the manner in which that
October 28, 1971

item is administered at present by the Department of National Revenue. I do not note any significant change in the bill on that particular item. I can only say I am confident that the Minister of National Revenue will receive reasonable representations in this regard from taxpayers who feel aggrieved. He may, indeed, be able to point out to the hon. members who questioned the matter the fact that perhaps there is more than one side to some of the representations that are being made.
Different sizes of stomachs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The expenses of an employee working away from home and going home on weekends was raised by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. He suggested that it might be covered under the provisions of section 8 (h) of the bill. I suggest that probably he is stretching 8 (h) if he thinks that it will go that far.
The hon. member for Regina East raised the question of transportation of handicapped persons to and from work. This, again, is a difficult subject. I think it was dealt with in essence in our debate on section 110, and I would refer the hon. member to the various improvements that are made in this bill in section 110 as opposed to the existing act when it comes to deductions for medical expenses and the other very well deserved concessions to handicapped persons.
The hon. member for Dauphin raised the matter of the carry forward of losses from employment under section 5(2). I would suggest with respect that the hon. member is in error in suggesting that a loss from employment could not be carried forward or back in the same way as a business loss. I think he misunderstands the section, and I would refer him to section 111(b) at page 292 of the bill which contains the definition of non-capital loss and includes in that definition a loss from employment. A non-capital loss may be carried forward five years and back one year.
The hon. member for Edmonton West again raised the matter of ages under the bill. I must say that I am inclined to agree that he has a point in the allusion that he made to the age in section 63(a)(iii)(B), the baby sitting section. I did respond to his questions regarding section 109(l)(d) the other day. Evidently he did not hear me. I would refer him to my remarks rather than repeat them. When he studies them he might conclude that a change in that section would impose a heavier burden on taxpayers rather than be a relief. He might feel that a parent claiming an exemption for a child should not have to prove that a child between the age of 18 and 21 is either in an educational institution or handicapped in order to get that exemption.
You do now for those over 21.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is correct, but the change from 21 to 18 would mean that you would have to do it for those over 18 rather than 21, so perhaps it is not an improvement.
I would also draw the hon. member's attention to the change in section 75 dealing with the income from property, gifts to minors, and note that one of the government amendments presently before the House proposes to change the traditional age in that regard from 19 down to
Income Tax Act
18. There may be other sections but, as I said, I am inclined to think that the hon. member has a pretty good point on section 63.1 will call it to the minister's attention.
So far as section 4(4) is concerned, the hon. member requested an explanation of that. Again, on reflection I would think that he should appreciate that this is a clarifying section which is desirable from the taxpayers point of view. It makes clear that an amount does not have to be included in income more than once, and also of course that a deduction cannot be taken more than once in the computation of income or loss. The reason for this is the considerable amount of emphasis throughout the bill, and particularly in this subdivision of the bill, on the sources of income. It is important to make sure that an item of income that is included from one source does not, by some technicality or other, have to be included again, and likewise that a deduction taken from one source of income cannot also be claimed against another source of income. It may be overly fastidious to have included this but it is a clarifying rather than a substantive section. I will check the inventory again. I hope I have caught up all the loose ends. If I have not, I will certainly try to do so.

May I raise a point of order at this time? My point of order arises out of something which the parliamentary secretary said with regard to the representation that I made and which the hon. member for Lamb-ton-Kent and others made about the mamma and papa provision which is contained in section 6(8). I think the parliamentary secretary made a reasonable representation and it would be agreeable I think that we deal with that later on. I hope we will always have the wisdom, if it turns out that section 6(8) is all that essential, to give ourselves leeway to come back and make any changes there. I should like to be heard later on about other matters arising out of the statement, but I realize that I am up on a point of order and I will not indulge myself now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would normally see the hon. member who is on his feet, but I think members of the committee will agree that because of the very useful line that the hon. member for Edmonton West took and which was responded to by the parliamentary secretary it would facilitate the work of the committee if I were now to see the hon. member for Edmonton West.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I will not abuse this privilege. Actually, I do not think I will use all of the time allotted to me.
I should like to return to section 6(l)(a). This provision includes in an employee's income an employer's contribution to public health schemes, but only on the basis that the benefit under the scheme depends on the employer making the contribution. In other words, in the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta under the medicare schemes presently in force, because the employer has to participate by way of an agreement in a contribution to the scheme, the employee receives a taxable benefit to the extent of the employer's contribution. But strangely enough in the province of Quebec there is no question of agreement or otherwise. The employer's contribution to medicare is by way of a separate tax under a provincial

October 28, 1971
Income Tax Act
statute. Therefore we find there is a distinction, between one part of the country and another, for employees receiving the same sort of benefit. In Quebec, the employer must contribute to the medicare scheme. In Ontario, as a result of collective bargaining, the employer has to contribute to the medicare scheme. In the province of Alberta and in the province of British Columbia the employee has to pay for it, by reason of an addition to his income at the margin on which he will pay marginal rates.
I just cannot see that as equity between taxpayers, and after all the government did say that one of the things it was striving for was equity between taxpayers. I do not disagree that you can handle taxpayers differently, but do not tell us you are going to handle them the same way. It seems to me that to determine the tax consequences to an employee on the wording of a provincial statute is absolutely the wrong way to proceed in a federal statute. And let us not hear any nonsense that the provinces should change their medicare schemes, to make the premiums under medicare a complete charge to the consolidated revenue fund of the provinces, in order to do away with this. There was never a condition precedent under any medicare scheme that such should be the case. To try to force this through the Income Tax Act is totally wrong and is, in effect, saying it is up to the provincial administration to change the set up.
Why not tax the employee in Quebec for the value of the tax paid by the employer towards the medicare scheme? It is a payment for the benefit of the employee. But because it is a tax, apparently the department doesn't want to do it, or are they scared to do it?
Maybe both.

If it is fair to tax an Ontario employee for the benefit of his employer's contribution to a medicare premium under a provincial statute, or in Alberta or British Columbia, then it is equally fair to tax the one in Quebec. If you are not going to do it for the Quebec employee, then you should not do it for the others. But for goodness sake, treat that category of employees who are receiving part of their premiums under a medicare scheme from an employer equally and not as proposed in this bill.
I would like now to turn to the employment expense deduction. Here, I find some real anomalies. I am not going to say anything about the amount of $150, whether it is right or wrong. I am not going to say anything about whether it should be provided or should not be provided. Frankly, I do not particularly care that it should be provided. I have never been a great devotee of this particular feature because it seems to me that it discriminates, and it confers on certain employees a benefit to which they are not entitled.
When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was speaking yesterday I gave him examples of what I considered to be anomalies. You may say that a $150 employment expense deduction for the office boy and junior stenographers in a large concern would be most welcome. I am sure they will welcome it, but if you take the case of a $75,000 a year president of a company, he too will be entitled to the $150. The president of the Canadian National, the president of the CBC and the Governor of the Bank of Canada will all be entitled to this $150. Every deputy

minister is an employee entitled to it, unless such individual has an otherwise tax free allowance, such as a Member of Parliament, a city alderman, or member of a provincial legislature. Those individuals do not qualify, but all others who are employees qualify. The $150 for the man whose marginal rate is 40 per cent or 50 per cent is pretty nice, but for the man or woman whose marginal rate is 15 per cent or 17 per cent the deduction from total income really means a saving of very little, because this $150 is not deductible from your tax. This $150 is deductible from gross income.
I find these flat rate deductions to be wrong in principle, the same way that I find a flat rate exemption allowance creates some great disparities. Why do you do this? Let me give an example of it in my own profession, that of a lawyer. We will take a large law firm with a great number of staff lawyers. They will all be entitled to the working allowance. But just down the corridor are a couple of struggling young lawyers who will not be entitled to any of these travelling or employment expenses because they are self-employed.
They deduct their own expenses.

They cannot. This allowance will go toward the cost of travelling back and forth to the job for a stenographer or an office boy or the worker in a factory, because it is known as an employment expense deduction. In the same bus or subway car will be the self-employed lawyer or accountant-the hon. member for Laurier should know and should stand up for his profession-but they cannot qualify.
He can charge his expenses.
He cannot charge those expenses travelling from his home to his place of business. Certainly, no lawyer can.
He has the compensation there.

There is this discrimination between the two. The hon. member for Laurier should know better. I am speaking from personal experience, in my profession as a staff lawyer in a large law firm, of what is allowed and what is not allowed as an employment expense. I can also speak about the nonsense of a self-employed lawyer attending a bar convention or the Canadian Tax Foundation. When a lawyer who is a Member of Parliament attends these seminars in order to keep up to date, he cannot deduct his expenses because his profession is not his principal source of income.
I agree with that.

I think the hon. member for Laurier will see that there is this discrimination between the lawyer who is working for a large law firm and the one who is on his own. He cannot deduct his travelling expenses from his home to his place of business, that is for sure. I have said enough on this occasion, Mr. Chairman. I thank hon. members for allowing me this extra time and you, Mr. Chairman, for recognizing me so quickly. It may be that I will come back with further points on this section.
October 28, 1971

Mr. Chairman, a pattern seems to be emerging on the employment expense allowance, particularly after listening to the hon. parliamentary secretary. Interestingly enough, and I think honestly enough, he pointed out that there has always been inequity in our tax system regarding the deduction of employment expenses as far as the employee is concerned as against the deduction of employment expenses for the self-employed person and the proprietor, and that the government has been grappling with this problem for a long time but has not been able to sort it out. The argument presented against equity as between the employee and the proprietor is that there are fewer proprietors and more employees, therefore trying to treat them on an equal basis poses an insurmountable problem. The parliamentary secretary says that the government has moved to put a little more equity into the situation by allowing a ceiling of $150 for employment expenses.
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, that looks like the worst kind of tax gerrymandering. Whichever way you look at what the government has done, it means that virtually all adults in our society will be able to make this $150 deduction and those who cannot, those outside the labour force because of age, are taken care of because $100 has been added to the $500 previously allowed as a deduction at age 70, now reduced to age 65. The government has not moved to correct the basic inequity in the system. Instead of increasing the amount that each individual could use as a base for deduction, instead of raising the ceiling of the single exemption to $2,000 and the married exemption to $4,000 for income tax purposes, they have taken $150 out of that and applied it to this section. If you were to calculate what it would have cost if the amount of the basic exemptions had been raised as against what it is going to cost this way, I think there would have been very little difference.
They have gerrymandered the thing around. There is a certain amount of money for disbursal and they have decided that, rather than use it to grant increased exemptions, they would use it to grant an employment allowance. I am not impressed with that approach because we are still faced with the basic inequity and all the apologies from the parliamentary secretary, all the hand wringing about how difficult it is to accomplish anything in that area, leaves me cold. I think it will leave the vast majority of people the same way.
As a rule, it is the little things that are very annoying. There is one subsection in section 6 which allows employees the right to deduct the cost of selling their product or advancing the interest of their company. Now that has always been deductible. But what is not taken into account is that almost all working men in this country at one time or another have to seek new employment or seek to improve their position. In this sense, they are not different from the person who is looking for business, who is selling a product. But the cost of finding a job cannot be deducted. If a man has been phased out of one industry and has to travel all over the city or buy three newspapers to look for a job-and under present conditions of high unemployment he may spend a fair amount of time and money trying to relocate-these expenses are not deductible. In a sense, he is in the business of providing his own labour; that is all he has to sell. He does not
Income Tax Act
have a product or a service to sell, just himself. Yet there is no provision for him to deduct the cost of finding employment. This is simply an indication of how callous our tax system is, Mr. Chairman, how indifferent to the needs of the majority of taxpayers and how solicitous it is of those who are self-employed or the proprietors of businesses.
The government acknowledges that the system of employment expenses is inequitable, but even if it is so difficult to bring equity into the tax system is it necessary to carry on this injustice against the larger group of our population. Something more should be done than to offer apologies. The government has one or two choices open to it. Most people will not claim beyond the $150. They ought to set up the necessary administration, as they have done with respect to business concerns and self employed people, in order to process those extraordinary expenses that some workers incur in finding and holding employment. Those expenses ought to be processed on the same basis as other, similar expenses are processed.
On the other hand, if the administrative problems that this would create are too great, then the government should move in the other direction and disallow all such expenses. In other words, there ought to be no allowances for expenses incurred in business; neither the salesman's nor the steel worker's expenses ought to be deductible. I am sure that vast sums of money are lost from our national revenues through the ability of business concerns to deduct from taxes the cost of doing business. If all such expenses were disallowed, we would introduce some form of equity. The money that is saved could be applied to everybody's marginal rate of tax. All taxes could be reduced and there would be a return to equity. I find it impossible to accept the government's explanation, namely, that although the present practice is inequitable we have no choice except to proceed as we always have.
Since the parliamentary secretary has been so good about answering questions that have been raised in this debate, could he say whether the government has calculated how much revenue is lost as a result of allowing business expenses to be tax deductible? If those amounts were not allowed, what amount of revenue would be available for lowering everyone's marginal rate of tax?

Is the parliamentary secretary ready? I should like to know whether the government has calculated how much revenue is lost as a result of allowing these expenses to be tax deductible. In other words, what revenue would be saved if there were no deductions for business expenses, travelling expenses as well as the expenses of employment? What amount of revenue would be available to the government if those deductions were disallowed and what kinds of tax changes could be made in the marginal rates of taxpayers if that amount were applied equally to all people for that purpose?

If he cannot make the calculation on the basis of all business expenses, could he deal with expenses connected with the cost of employment or the costs of doing business that may be compared to the costs that the workman must meet for holding down his job?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that I do not know of any such calculation having been made. I have grave doubts as to whether it has been made. I will look at the hon. member's question in Hansard and see if we can get any information for the hon. member. I am not aware of that calculation having been made and, as I say, I have grave doubts as to whether it has been made.
That shows what is wrong with the system.

Mr. Chairman, I am somewhat puzzled by the reply of the parliamentary secretary. We are asked to approve a clause in this comprehensive bill which would permit workers, as well as other citizens, to deduct the magnificent amount of $150 a year for expenses connected with their work. This is not a new subject. Members of my party as well as of other parties have raised this question over many years, namely, that many ordinary workers working for wages and many people who work for salaries pay substantially more than $150 a year directly in expenses relating to their work.
The hon. member for Waterloo talked about costs incurred by the worker who has been laid off and must drive hundreds of miles to a prospective employer in order to find another job. Yet there are tens of thousands of workers who drive between 25 and 100 miles every day to and from work. Until now, they have not been able to deduct five cents of those expenses from taxable income. Thousands of construction workers must buy their own tools. Until now, they have not been able to deduct the cost of those tools from taxable income when calculating income tax. Thousands of miners cannot go into mines unless they wear hard hats and safety boots, which they must buy themselves. Those items cost something, and the cost has not been deductible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is precisely why we are allowing the $150.

The parliamentary secretary has always understood clearly the position of the salaried person who travels as a salesman or of the self-employed person, with whom I shall be dealing in a moment. The parliamentary secretary interjected just now to suggest that the government is allowing $150 to cover such expenses as I have mentioned. I say to the parliamentary secretary that $150 sometimes may be too much and sometimes it may not be enough. I say to him that I believe in equity. I think the worker is entitled to nothing more and to nothing less than the kind of consideration which, for many years,

Canadian governments have extended to businessmen and self-employed persons. The businessman who thinks he will get more business if he takes a prospective customer out to dinner never has to prove that he got the business from that prospective customer. If he decides to take the customer to lunch or dinner at the Chateau Laurier, the Skyline Hotel, the Queen Elizabeth Hotel in Montreal, the Royal York Hotel in Toronto or the Palliser Hotel in the parliamentary secretary's home city of Calgary, nobody asks questions. The businessman charges the expense as a business expense, and the lunch or dinner does not cost him anything. If he decides to go to another city because he can get some business there and he flies first class, stays at the best hotel and eats the best meals available, he can charge the cost of the trip as a business expense.
Towards which the worker pays his share.

I ought to say that 50 per cent of the cost is paid for by the people of Canada. Let us take the case of the doctor who decides to attend a convention that is being held in the field in which he specializes. The convention may be held on a cruise ship cruising the Caribbean. Of course, there are meetings, the doctor listens to lectures and acquires more information in the field in which he specializes.
Union executives do that, too.

My hon. friend says that union executives do that, too. However, that sort of thing is not part of their duties. Unions, to my knowledge, are not in the business of making profits and taxpayers do not pay for such things. The members of the union may pay, or they may object. The taxpayer does not pay. If the union member does not like it, he can do something about it. The taxpayer can only do something about that sort of practice if we, in this chamber, do something about it. That is what I am trying to impress on the parliamentary secretary. We are trying to persuade him in this matter but I must admit I do not think we have much hope of succeeding. The point I am trying to make is that for years we have permitted business, self-employed and professional people to escape payment of very substantial taxes because of these loopholes. I am not talking about tax evasion. I am talking about provisions in the income tax laws. This is a very small group, certainly less than 10 per cent of the people of Canada.
I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that it is time the ordinary workingman was given the same kind of advantage. I find it hard to understand why it should be so difficult to accomplish that objective. In fact, the government says it is impossible to set up a system of accounting or bookkeeping which will permit the ordinary workingman to do this. It has never been difficult for the doctor, lawyer or businessman to do that. A lawyer may travel in his car from the west end of Ottawa to a new office building downtown, then to the court house, which is not very far, back to his office and then home. He can charge a substantial part of his automobile expenses in the year when calculating his income tax.
October 28, 1971

I admit that I am ignorant about financial matters. I would like the parliamentary secretary to tell me why the government has been able to arrive at a decision that it is right, proper and equitable for that type of person to charge these expenses against his income tax, while it is not possible to do anything more for the workingman than to allow him a flat rate of $150. In thousands of cases, this is not adequate. The parliamentary secretary has some high priced help sitting with him at the table. Why can they not spend some time devising a system which will give the same treatment to the ordinary workingman who earns $5,000 or $6,000 a year? For years there has been such a system for business and professional men in the $25,000 to $50,000 a year bracket. When the parliamentary secretary explains that to my satisfaction, he will not hear another word about that from me and this section will carry very quickly.

My remarks will probably be redundant, Mr. Chairman, but I think what I have to say must be said. I was surprised at the statement made by the parliamentary secretary in answer, to the question he was asked by the hon. member for Waterloo. The hon. member asked the parliamentary secretary to calculate what would happen if we cut off the dishonest and supernumerary allowances which are now classified as expenses. He referred to the free automobile, free meals and all other such expenditures. He asked what amount of revenue would be available for the reduction of the tax if those expenses were not allowed.
I am curious, Mr. Chairman. I am probably stupid about finances. I am in the same position as many other members who set up a company. I have a small operation and I also have a farm. It is not difficult for me to write off $3,000 or $4,000 when calculating my income tax. I spend a little money and increase my capital value. I could write that off. I maintain a truck, tractor and considerable other equipment. There would be no problem writing off those items. However, I consider that to be morally wrong. I could hire an accountant just to cheat the government, but that would be morally wrong. Just because I have the machinery and know how to do it, I can get a deduction off my taxes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: But you do it.

No, I do not. My deductions at the present time are $1,000 for my wife, the $100 exemption everyone is allowed and the deduction for pension. These are the only exemptions I take. I could write off $4,000 or $5,000 if I wished, but I consider that dishonest. When I attend a large restaurant in Ottawa, I see that everyone there except myself and maybe one or two others are on expense accounts. That is more than dishonest, it is downright disgusting. I have to pay at least twice what the meal is worth because the freeloaders are riding on me and all other taxpayers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? In what category does the hon. member regard his tax free allowance as a member of Parliament in relation to all these freeloaders in the Skyline Hotel?

That is a simple question. If the hon. member did not have such a large income from other
Income Tax Act
sources, he would be aware of the answer. That exemption covers exactly what it was intended to cover, namely moneys normally expended by any member on behalf of his constituents that would not be expended in any other occupation. It is granted in lieu of increasing our salaries, and I do not think it is dishonest. Parliament passed it. It is a fair amount. You can argue one way or another about the $2,000. Some members are cheap about spending the $8,000, but I think it is safe to say that all members who a few years ago were able to live on their salary had to dig into that expense allowance to maintain themselves. In the main, those businessmen who are allowed to write off expenses such as meals are dishonest. Everyone in this country knows that 50 per cent of them are dishonest because the expenses are not justified. If the department wishes, it could curtail those expenses by at least 50 per cent and gain on revenue.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Canadian Pacific Oil and Gas Company, which really owns this particular company, is accepting these changes. Central-Del Rio is now going out of business and will hereafter be called the Pan-Canadian Oil Company. I anticipate this will be a consortium of companies taking in many of the other subsidiaries which have been mentioned as being under the control of this company.
Therefore, I think that this company should be congratulated for having taken the stand it has, one in which I am sure all members of the House are interested, namely that its directors will be resident in Canada. Hopefully it follows that this company will have a Canadian interest in its deliberations and in its day to day operations, particularly since the Gray report has not yet been released. It is to be hoped that that report will come before Parliament in the very near future, since it is vitally important that the government state its position on Canadian control of companies.
We may be naive enough to think that control rests with the board of directors and shareholders of a company. However, if the government gives leadership and shows what it wants accomplished in Canada, then a company like Central-Del Rio will not itself have to show the leadership that is required in this regard. There are other bills of a similar nature on the order paper, and if these companies wish to follow Central-Del Rio and make the same kind of concession to Canadian nationalism, then I think they will find much less difficulty getting their bills through this place.
I therefore express the hope that the government will introduce a policy establishing Canadian control of corporations, rather than asking individual companies to make this decision which, from a legal point of view, I am sure must have been difficult to make. Nevertheless, this company should be congratulated for having made that decision. As I say, I think there is now an obligation on the government not to place companies in the position of having to come before Parliament to get Canadian control. If the government shows leadership it will accomplish what the Gray report would accomplish by giving that direction which hitherto has been lacking.

Mr. Speaker, I do not like to be the sceptic here and I am not familiar with the original bill or the amendments made to it. I also kept my silence when they were explained to the House. However, I cannot see that there is any real victory for Canadian ownership in having a company declare that its directors shall be Canadians. In fact, I think this has been the case with most foreign-controlled companies for a good many years. The directors of these companies are straw men in some cases and real directors in others. Just in which cases they are straw men and in which cases they are effective directors is hard for an outside observer to tell.
Therefore, while I accept that there has been a concession in this case to Canadian direction of this company, I am not caught up in the euphoria of thinking there has been any real accomplishment here beyond the simple
Income Tax Act
fact that this company must have Canadian directors. I think this is an acknowledgment of the need for legislation in this respect, and when it does come before the House I hope it will be a good deal more effective than legislation that merely provides that the directors of companies shall be Canadians.
I do not want to detract from the effort that has been made in this case because it is one step along the road. But as already pointed out by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), something a good deal more than this will have to come from any legislation to ensure that there is in fact real Canadian control.
