speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, just before we proceeded to private members' hour I was pointing out to the parliamentary secretary that workers at the lower end of the income scale have to pay the maximum amount of tax and are allowed only the stereotype deductions. That situation can in no way be related to the situation faced by people in other income categories. The parliamentary secretary suggested that if we allowed these deductions in all categories $280 million would be involved. It would be of tremendous advantage to the country if we could use that money in allowing the average worker to write off some of his expenses. If this cannot be done, then we should at least reduce some of the deduction items at the other end of the income scale.
Every time a businessman takes someone out for a meal we pay 50 per cent of the cost. If we have a meal in a

October 28, 1971
Income Tax Act
restaurant we are charged 50 per cent more than we should be because most people eating in restaurants are subsidized or are on expense accounts. I have never been convinced that anyone can increase his business by wining and dining potential customers. It seems to me that what is involved is the old theory of, you scratch my back and I'll scratch yours; I will take you out on my expense account and you can take me out on yours. All that is gained is a social evening. I fail to see the legitimacy of allowing this type of exemption when we will not allow such basic exemptions as the cost of travel from place to place in the course of employment.
It is very difficult to ascertain how much an individual should be allowed for expenses. I am sure that this situation has changed radically in the last few years, mainly as a result of government action. In many areas, mines are situated some distance from where miners live. It was decided some time ago that in the province of Ontario townsites should not be developed on mining property. This has been the case for the last 15 or 25 years. It was felt that the capital cost necessary to develop townsites might be better used if the miners lived in an existing centre and travelled from there to the mine. Capital has already been laid out to establish such towns and villages. This was not the case 20 years ago.
I lived in a mine townsite which was about a quarter of a mile from the mine. The mine was easy to reach on foot. Miners in my area today drive 100 miles to and from work. It seems to me very strange that people who have to drive to their jobs are not granted at least an expense allowance to cover their travelling costs.
A farmer would be allowed capital depreciation and all the cash necessary. Probably 5 per cent or 10 per cent would be allowed for personal expenses other than for the operation of the business. But so far as workers are concerned there is no allowance for capital expenditure on an automobile. No allowance is made for gasoline or other expenditures. As my colleague says, only the rich benefit from our tax laws. Is it not time we started to be fair with the working people of this country?
I have been impressed when the minister has said on a number of occasions that the basic exemption cannot be changed, that it cannot be raised because it would cost too much. I am aware that this would help the guy at the bottom, but it helps the guy in the high categories considerably more. Is it not an indication that the tax department has not done its job when we are not able to reclaim moneys in a fair manner under our tax structure? It has been said that we cannot pay more money to old age pensioners; our tax structure is so badly out of line that we cannot equitably recover the costs from the various income categories.
The government has been very generous and I am sure that government after government will say that $150 is only a foot in the door, that next time it will be $200 and then $250. They will play with the workers as though they were a political football; they will offer them a little here and a little there toward the cost of their tools. But I know of no group of workers in this country that is not willing to document the expenditures incurred in its trade. As a miner I would have been very happy to document the fact

that I paid $11 or $12 for a pair of boots necessary in my occupation, to pay the $9 or $10 for the hat necessary in my work, the $4 or $5 for a belt to carry the lamp which is necessary in my work, the $15, $18 or $20 for oilers and the $4 or $5 for neoprene gloves.
I would have been happy to document these expenses if I could have written them off as business expenditures- and in my opinion those were business expenditures. I could not work without this equipment and therefore it was necessary for my work. I think a government is pretty decadent, and so is the tax department, if they cannot see the justification in allowing workers to provide receipts for certain items which are necessary in carrying out their jobs. Yet we allow businessmen to spend all kinds of money on booze, food and women, on hotel rooms and vacations around the world. We allow this and each of us has to pay for it. It seems to me that a government that cannot make this distinction has not looked at the tax structure in the light of reform. I agree that the tax structure is incomprehensible to anyone and I think it is time there was some fairness in the exemptions that we allow.
With regard to the 3 per cent of income provision, I know of people who pay almost 10 per cent of their income in transportation costs alone and they have all the other disadvantages that go with carrying lunch-pails, eating a poor lunch and working overtime and eating a warmed-up TV dinner. I do not blame people who look at the balance-sheet and say it is costing them money to work and that they would be better off receiving welfare, and perhaps that is the alternative.
The only way in which this country will get ahead is for the working people to feel they are getting a fair break under the taxation structure. If workers know that the boss is cheating, that he has all kinds of ways of getting exemptions to which they are not entitled, they lose respect for the system and doubt the justice which everybody agrees should prevail.
I should like the parliamentary secretary to indicate that the government will consider allowing exemptions for travelling expenses if receipts are submitted. If necessary, these receipts or vouchers could be co-signed by the employer. If a person is travelling in somebody else's car, obviously they are entitled to only a share of the exemption. Most companies would be able to supervise this and there would be no need for a number of inspectors.
So far as the $150 is concerned, I say thank you very much but this is only a drop in the bucket for the people involved. The government does not ask a doctor whether he needs a new scalpel. They do not ask how much it cost; the doctor tells them how much it cost. The government does not check whether he needs three or six scalpels a year, and he does not have to provide receipts for them. He gives them a complicated breakdown of his office expenses and sometimes lets the inspector come in to look over the books. Every time, to my knowledge, they collect about three times the tax which the doctor estimated, so I expect that the receipts system in these cases is not very good.
Perhaps the parliamentary secretary doubts this, but I know of cases where inspectors have come in and taken out what I would consider to be considerably more than
October 28, 1971

the fellow was supposed to be making that year, without much squawking from the person concerned. If it is good for one person, why is it not good for another? Why do we always have to ask the little guy to pay the largest share? He does not necessarily pay the most money, but in terms of the income he receives he pays the major share. He will not be allowed to collect for his wife and for his children. He will now have an exemption of $100 for dues. The fact that he may have a strike assessment will not be taken into consideration. Now we are to make it a maximum of 3 per cent of his income or up to $150 to be deducted for tools.
The workers of this country are not getting a fair break.
I urge that they be given a fair break. We do not want to continue the inequitable system which favours the very rich who have cushy jobs. If we give them a concession, at least let us give the working people of this country an opportunity to get some benefits from their expenditures. They do not want these benefits so as to have a good time, to go out on Saturday night and drink beer at the Legion; they only want to cover their expenses in travelling from home to job and buying equipment which is necessary and which is becoming exceedingly costly. I think these are two provisions which could easily be amended. In the amended form they would receive the support of all sectors of our community.

Mr. Chairman, once more I would like to take a matter up strongly with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney). I do not know if he understood the intervention I made yesterday, but anyway several other members, among which the previous speaker, expressed the same opinion that clause 8 provides for something new, that is a tax deduction for employment expenses of not more than $150 that everyone can claim, even workers, loggers, miners and those who travel between their residence and their place of work.
I repeat what I said yesterday: the amount is minimal. It represents only 2 to 4 cents a mile. I think it is less than what it costs a worker to get to his work.
The buyer of an automobile pays the federal government a tax on car manufacturing and often, according to the province, a sales tax such as 8 per cent in Quebec and if he uses his car he must also pay substantial tax on the gas and oil he buys and on spare parts for the car he must maintain in good shape.
I think that the Department of Finance should in all justice for all Canadian workers revise that clause of the bill and allow a fair deduction for actual expenses claimed by the Canadian worker.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the discussion on section 4 we have also, of course, been considering sections 5, 6, 7 and 8. One of the points that has come in for a good deal of discussion has been the proposal to add an exemption of 3 per cent of income, or a limit of $150, which is said to be for employment expenses. I find it rather interesting to read the section in question, section 8. It starts at the bottom of page 15 of the
Income Tax Act
bill and goes over to page 16. You discover that in the text of the section it does not say what the expenses are for. However, the marginal note helps us out in this respect and I suppose in that sense it is part of the bill. The marginal note reads "Employment expense deduction."
We have been back and forth over this ground so it is hardly necessary to do it again in any kind of detail. But I had hoped that by now the government would have realized that it really is a little unfair for it not to relent at all on the basic system, namely, that of employing a tax exemption schedule rather than a tax credit system, and to add to the insult by providing this further exemption on that inequitable basis. After all, it is simply a case of an extra $150 exemption for all taxpayers in this country who get their income from employment. There is a slight qualification; persons who have some other tax-free allowance of $150 or more do not get it. We are glad to note that that includes Members of Parliament. But apart from those few exceptions which do not alter the picture greatly, all we have in this proposal is an additional $150 exemption for taxpayers who get their income from employment.
Whenever you do that sort of thing instead of putting it on a tax credit basis or without adjusting the rates, you are compounding the inequalities that already exist in our outdated tax law. As has been pointed out so many times, this $150 provision will mean a few dollars, $20 or $30 at most, to many of the workers of Canada when they fill out their income tax forms after next year is over. But the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the president of the Royal Bank of Canada and a few other big-shots will probably get 50 per cent or 60 per cent of the $150 exemption, which is $75 or more to them. It is a lot more than the little fellow gets-and these big-shots need an extra $75 a year just like a car needs a fifth wheel! Why can't we once in a while do this type of thing on the basis of fairness? We have not been able to persuade the government to change the basic system, but here a new element is being added. Why couldn't this be done on the basis of equity?
When I was speaking about this matter yesterday I referred to a situation that is at least slightly comparable, that of the allowance for charitable donations. I pointed out that in that case, as in at least one other, the government allows a $100 exemption to a taxpayer whether or not he has receipts for the charitable donations he has made. But the same taxpayer, if he has receipts, may claim more than $100. In that case there is another ceiling somewhere up the line. I suggested that that might be a pattern to follow in this case. I put it forward as reasonably as I could, hoping the government would reconsider it overnight and come back with such a proposal today. But whether it was considered overnight or not, it is not before us at this time-and I think it should be. As I said yesterday, let us accept the $150 for everyone, without any receipts, but why not provide that the worker who can furnish receipts for employment expenses be granted up to a total of $500?
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, since the government has not proposed this as an amendment to the bill-I confess I have not had time today to look at the further batch of amendments that we received at two o'clock this afternoon, but I am sure if one of those amendments had dealt with this matter word would have reached us by this

October 28, 1971
Income Tax Act
time-I would like to move an amendment along the lines which I suggested yesterday and to which I have just referred. I can see that Your Honour is wondering what is coming. Probably you can guess. I have already told you. I do not have another treatise on procedure. The other day I spent a great deal of time on a treatise on procedure and lost my amendment, but a colleague of mine rose later, offered an amendment, did not mention procedure and his amendment was accepted. So I think I should not argue; I should just present my amendment, listen to Your Honour say question, and get a vote on it.
However, I suppose Your Honour will look at my amendment and ask, "Doesn't that do something to the balance of ways and means?" Mr. Chairman, if you had been listening today to the parliamentary secretary you would have realized that those on the other side of the House are all at sea in this business of deductions for expenses: they don't quite know what it amounts to or how much you gain or lose. I suggest that if we gave the workers this extra allowance for expenses that they can document by receipts, it might result in the purchase of more tools and equipment. Then the people who sell the tools and equipment would make more profit, would pay more taxes and the government would probably be better off.
Since my argument in the direct field of procedure did not work the other day, I am trying this one on for size. Just because I am going to propose that workers be granted up to $500 rather than $150 by way of an expense allowance I do not think the Chair should just jump on it and say that it upsets the balance of ways and means. That is not necessarily so. It may in the end put money in the government's pocket. In any event, I think the committee should have the amendment before it. I have several copies and I can send one over to the parliamentary secretary and he can get one of the ministers sitting behind him to move it, if Your Honour finds it procedurally difficult. I am sure that by now they are feeling a bit sheepish about the inequity and unfairness of this $150 proposal. Therefore, I move:
That Bill C-259 be amended at page 16, in line 3, by changing the semicolon at the end of the said line 3 to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"provided however that the amount deductible under this paragraph may be an amount up to but not greater than $500, if payment of employment expenses for the total amount claimed is proven by filing receipts with the minister;".
I point out that if these words were added at the end of line 3 on page 16, then section 8(l)(a)(ii) would provide for a deduction which, abbreviated, would read: a single amount in respect of all offices and employments of the taxpayer, equal to the lesser of $150 and 3 per cent-
Then there are a number of lines simply referring to income. My words would be added at that point and would say that despite that limit of $150 and 3 per cent, the amount deductible under this paragraph may be an amount up to but not greater than $500, if payment of employment expenses for the total amount claimed is proven by filing receipts with the minister. One other comment I wish to make is that the language I have chosen at the end of the amendment is that which appears

in this bill in several places, namely, that where receipts are required it is proposed that they be receipts filed with the minister which prove the expense.
Also, in this bill in various places are provisions for the making of regulations, sometimes by the Minister of Finance and sometimes by the Minister of National Revenue. As I see it, there would have to be regulations, just as there are now regulations, about the receipts that one can file for charitable donations, the required numbers and all the rest of it. The general authority to deal with certain matters by regulation would cover the right of the government through one department or another to indicate what kind of expense could be claimed and the nature of the receipts to be submitted.
However, apart from the two questions I have raised about the regularity which I contend for this motion, and apart from the attempt I have made to show how it is put together, I plead basic fairness. There is no reference in the text itself to employment expense; that is found only in the marginal note. All that tells us is that the text itself has nothing to say about employment expenses, it is just a $150 deduction. But if the government is going to call it by its marginal note, that is, an employment expense deduction, let us have a section on it and make reference, as I do in my amendment, to employment expenses. Let us also do the fair thing and make the same amount available, if he spends the money, up to $500 for the worker in the mine, the worker who has to travel or anyone else regardless of the total income of that person.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in the name of equity for at least this part of the tax bill I propose the amendment which I have already read.
Question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Chair is not prepared to put the question at this time. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to the amendment moved by his colleague, the hon. member for Regina East. I would not want the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to think that because he moves an amendment the Chair is automatically on guard. This may be a logical conclusion to draw; however, the Chair can find a distinction. I accepted the amendment of the hon. member for Regina East the other evening on the basis of Beauchesne's citation which says that it is open to members to reduce taxes.
I would accept such an amendment if it were, shall I say, to reduce taxes across the board.
The difficulty I have with the amendment now before the committee is that if I permitted it and it were carried, it would shift the incidence of taxation. I am speaking now only on the procedural aspect and not on the fairness or moral aspect, as the hon. member urged on me-I make no decision on that. It seems to me, on the procedural aspect, that if this amendment were adopted there would be a shift in the incidence of taxation. There would in fact be an infringement on the financial initiative of the Crown. That is my preliminary thought on the matter. If the amendment were carried, of course, the situation would be that some taxpayers would pay less taxes and others would pay more.
I make this preliminary observation. If hon. members wish to try to convince me otherwise, I will listen to their
October 28, 1971

arguments, otherwise I would regretfully have to rule the amendment out of order.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should say that you have not taken me by surprise but I do not see how you can put much weight on the argument that my amendment shifts the incidence of taxation. In order to contend that, of course, I may have to contend that it simply reduces the total amount of taxes that has to be paid in.
The argument that a proposition shifts the incidence from one group to the other perhaps applied to the motion I made the other day when I tried to raise the exemption levels and thus take taxation off those on the lower end of the scale and put the tax on those at the higher end. This amendment simply takes the taxation off the workers who can submit vouchers for up to $500. As for the question of whether or not it is across the board, I think it is: it would apply to the worker at the lower end of the scale and to the governor of the Bank of Canada if he could submit vouchers for expenses up to $500.
On the other question, all I can say is I think there is no proof at all that this kind of amendment would result in any loss of income to the treasury and it would be much fairer to the workers of this country.
Question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The concern that the Chair has, of course, is not really cleared by the hon. member's remarks, because if his amendment were adopted I think we would be in the position that those taxpayers who are employees would have the benefit of the amendment. The situation is that there are other Canadians who are not employees, they are self-employed, so that the benefit that could accrue under this amendment to Canadians who are not self-employed but are employees would be borne by Canadians who are self-employed.
As I said, the argument of the hon. member may be morally or reasonably correct-although I make no comment on that-but I suggest it is not procedurally correct and a private member cannot, as the hon. member seeks to do, interfere with the financial initiative of the Crown by shifting the incidence of taxation. For example, if all Canadians were employed, then I think I could agree with the hon. member's argument. Some Canadians, however, are not employees; they are self-employed and thus would not have the benefit of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Therefore, those who are self-employed would, it seems to me, be carrying an additional burden.
I think, with respect, that the hon. member is doing something that can only be done under the financial initiative of the Crown. Accordingly, and regretfully, I must rule that the hon. member's motion is out of order.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the Minister of National Revenue, who represents that great, industrial city of Windsor, if he would not like to adopt this amendment and move it on behalf of the workers of that city as well as on behalf of all the workers of Canada?
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the proposal is a step forward, and the best way to help the workers in this regard is to pass this proposal of the government which is before the committee as quickly as possible.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the minister if what he said has become government policy?
Repeat that.
Has what the minister said become government policy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I was talking about the measure that the government has proposed to the House and that is before the committee, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I want to go on a voyage of discovery for a few moments and refer to some matters which have been raised in the House a number of times. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary could advise me whether some of these questions have been dealt with, because that may save some debating time.
Some time ago a representation was made to the government involving the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Employees Association. It came to the attention of many members of the House and had to do with the different ways in which people who work on different types of construction jobs are treated. For instance, we are told that expenses incurred by people who work on a new construction site can be included as tax deductible, whereas if workers do repair work on the same type of installation, or on annexes, elevators and the like, their expenses are not deductible.
Could the parliamentary secretary advise us whether there have been changes in the way this law has been interpreted? Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue could say whether there have been changes in the regulations under the pertinent sections. Those who are concerned would appreciate this information.
It appears that the government is completely insensitive to the whole area of expenses incurred by people working away from home. We have tried to suggest that certain matters could be included within the law and the government has suggested that if you open the door at all there will be no end to what will be asked. In this situation employees who are discriminated against are those who undertake repair work on certain annexes and elevators across the country. It appears that the criteria for determining their eligibility to deduct expenses are based solely upon the definition of work performed.
Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue or the parliamentary secretary could indicate whether change is to be expected in this area. I do not think consideration is being given to it. Members of this committee want the government to explain why such expenses should not be deductible for tax purposes. It seems to me that we are discriminating against people whose work is exactly the same as that of others whose expenses are tax deductible and who are employed on new construction.
I am sure the parliamentary secretary, who comes from western Canada, well knows that people who are repairing elevators are doing the same work as those who are

October 28, 1971
Income Tax Act
building new elevators and that they are entitled to the same type of treatment. After all, they are doing the same type of work. Why cannot both groups of people be treated equally? I ask the parliamentary secretary to tell us why employees doing similar jobs cannot be treated the same way.
Another area that has been debated at length-some of our arguments go back to the 1960's; one letter on the subject was written in 1967-is that of travelling expenses of those employed in construction, transportion or other, allied trades. This afternoon the parliamentary secretary suggested that this involves a personal situation, that it is the obligation of workers to move from their homes to their places of work. Those engaged in the various trades in this country are faced with a high degree of mobility, I agree; yet we can cite instances-I will use Canadian Pacific Railway and Canadian Pacific Express as examples-to show that because workers lack the necessary seniority in their respective terminals they must travel many miles in order to obtain employment.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration has told us how important manpower training and retraining is for Canadians. Representations in this area have been made to the Minister of National Revenue. There is a letter from the Minister of Finance saying that the subject of expenses incurred in earning salary and wages is receiving careful study during the current review of the income tax law. Surely when people cannot gain employment in their trades within their own terminals, places of origin or domicile and must travel "X" miles to obtain employment, consideration ought to be given to the deduction from taxable income of their travelling expenses.
I agree that if it appears that such people will become permanently employed at the new location, they ought to move to that location. In the long run this is what they will do and thus they will no longer pay travelling expenses. Yet somewhere along the line consideration ought to be given to allowing such travelling expenses for a certain length of time, especially in cases where people cannot get jobs in their own terminals or places of domicile. Consideration ought to be given to allowing some type of mileage charge in computing travelling expenses in cases where people must travel to another terminal or location for work. After all, they have to obtain food and shelter and keep up their homes. No consideration has been given to such people. Even now, one group can obtain concessions so far as expenses are concerned yet others who work under similar circumstances are denied these concessions. Consideration ought to be given to those so affected.
May I refer briefly of situations existing in the railway industry. I am sure that the parliamentary secretary, who comes from the city of Calgary, knows many railroaders in that city. We know that with the type of seniority prevailing on the railroads some people are forced to go away from home to obtain employment. If they want to work they must travel many miles to another location. At one time the railway companies themselves provided accommodation for their employees. Today those who are forced away from home for work invariably must obtain their own accommodation and pay their living costs at the work terminals.
I am glad that in the bill there is provision for an exemption in so far as telegraphers' and station agents' expenses are concerned. I would like to know why the government cannot include in those exemptions the expenses of employees working away from home terminals because they have exercised their seniority. The parliamentary secretary is well aware that people from Calgary go to Red Deer to work. They have to pay their own expenses. No consideration is given to that type of expense. If the parliamentary secretary would answer this question right now it would be appreciated by all those affected.
We witness the disappearance of passenger trains throughout the country. It used to be that running trade employees could go to away-from-home terminals by train, but now that is practically impossible. They have to use their own automobiles to travel to away-from-home terminal for employment. They receive no consideration for expenses incurred in this way. Again we are faced with the situation where you have two sets of conditions. There are people with ability and seniority who work within their own territory. Others have the same ability but not the seniority and are forced to go away from home in order to obtain employment. Surely there could be some amendment or a few words added to the clause at the top of page 17 to include the running trades to which I am referring.
The same applies to the non-operating trades. They have what they call roving gangs. These people no longer have a domicile to call their own and are used throughout the territory. They are in the same situation of having to drive from one location to the other but receive no consideration so far as tax exemption is concerned. Possibly the government would agree to add a few words to this clause to look after the situation with which these people are faced. I do not see any object in trying to move an amendment to include this group of people unless it includes construction workers, railway workers and other trades and craftsmen.
If these people were included, their legitimate expenses could no doubt be documented to the extent that the government would know how much money was spent. As far as blanket coverage is concerned, I agree that this is not in the interest of the Income Tax Act. If legitimate expenses were documented I see no reason why these people would not be entitled to consideration under the proposed changes.
Over the past few years the Minister of Finance has suggested that these areas were being considered. I think he was sincere when he said that at the time the Income Tax Act was to be revised and revamped. When I look through it I see that the three areas to which I have referred are not included. No consideration given to these situations. With regard to people in the construction industry and railway industry, I think some words should be added to the legislation to cover the situation. I leave it at that. Possibly the parliamentary secretary, who is well versed in the Calgary situation where there are very many railroad people, has received representations. I am sure he is aware of the problems I have recited.

October 28, 1971

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am indeed, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member has asked a couple of very specific questions that might as well be answered now as later. On the matter of employee expenses, the hon. member cited the problem experienced by contractors' employees who are away from home building grain elevators and employees of grain companies out on maintenance and repair work.
If the hon. member examines section 6(6) of the bill I think he will be satisfied that that particular anomaly has been removed. Workers who are employed away from home on repairs will now be in a position where the payments made to them by their employer for living expenses away from home will not have to be included in income. There is a distinction that is important. The employee is not entitled to deduct from his income his personal expenses. It is a matter of an employer making him an allowance to cover those expenses while he is away from his home base. In those circumstances that allowance is no longer an income item.
With regard to travelling expenses, Mr. Chairman, I am sorry the response to the hon. member cannot be as favourable, at least from his point of view. The government has not yet satisfied itself as to an equitable means of permitting people to deduct the expenses of travelling to and from work. This applies as much to travelling to and from work ten miles across the city, 20 miles down the road on a daily basis or, indeed, as do some of our top executives-for whom I am sure the hon. member is not speaking-flying across the country two or three times a week while locating in a new job and trying to find a house in a new location. No satisfactory answer to this, at least from the hon. member's point of view, has been found. However, I should point out that under section 62 the transfer costs of the employee moving from one location to another are covered when he actually moves his home to the site of his new employment. Was there another point?

Yes, there was, Mr. Chairman. Can the parliamentary secretary elaborate on his statement that the government is not really satisfied with the answer of the travel allowance? Where is it going and when are we to have an answer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Chairman; I am not quite clear on the purport of the question.

I think the parliamentary secretary said that the government is not really satisfied with the answer it has with regard to travel allowances. Are special studies being carried on, or is this where the matter rests? He sounded very frank. I wonder where this frankness will lead us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the government is and will continue to review the matter. The dissatisfaction to which I alluded was the fact that I was afraid I could not provide the hon. member for Moose Jaw with an answer that would satisfy him.

Mr. Chairman, the real question, as the parliamentary secretary suggested, is that section 62 takes into account the transfer cost from one home to another. He is missing the point that their seniority is established in a particular terminal. If these people transfer every

time they have to move 140 miles to another terminal in order to gain employment, they will be transferring back and forth all the time. It is this situation about which the railway brotherhood is concerned, as well as employees who are involved in this type of transfer.

Mr. Chairman, may I clearly express the position of the New Democratic Party on employment expenses. We have said that all legitimate expenses that can be documented by receipts or standard deductions be allowed as a deductible item, and I think that is a fair position to take. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre attempted to reach a compromise position this evening by moving an amendment to the effect that we change the existing clause to provide that where receipts are supplied by a worker, the deductions should be to a maximum of $500. That amendment was rejected.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The rules of the House clearly prohibit hon. members from referring to a decision made by the House or even commenting on a decision of the House. The reason we in the New Democratic Party believe that all legitimate employment expenses should be deducted is that in urban centres we find that many major industries have moved from the core of the city to its suburbs. Many of the workers have bought homes in the core of the city, and having established themselves and their families in the downtown area now find themselves in the position where if they wish to retain their employment they must travel to the plant out in the suburbs. They thereby incur additional employment expenses.
It can easily be argued that perhaps these workers should move from the centre of the city to an area closer to the plant in the suburbs. Many of them cannot do this because of their age. They have worked hard to save sufficient money to purchase a home. Having purchased
October 28, 1971

the home they have paid off their mortgage over a long period of years.
By blood, sweat and tears.

As the hon. member for Hamilton West says, by blood, sweat and tears. That is true, but what is even more true is that by moving from the centre of the city closer to the plant in the suburbs they have to buy a new home at a highly inflated price and assume a mortgage at an interest rate that ranges from 9 per cent up. I realize that the Secretary of state who is in charge of urban affairs is not happy about the high interest rates in the housing field, but the position of these employees has to be brought home to the government, and brought home forcefully. This is why I want members from the urban centres to speak to this matter.
Many of these workers are being penalized for living in the centre of a city. Is it unreasonable to ask the parliamentary secretary or the government to take these representations into account and to permit these workers to deduct their reasonable travelling expenses occasioned by going from their homes to their place of work in the suburbs? This is why we in the New Democratic Party contend that all legitimate expenses that are substantiated by receipts should be deducted.
Mr. Chairman, I have always found you a man of fairness. I have found some members of the Liberal party men of fairness. Yet in some debates I find these men sitting idly by when crucial matters which affect their constituents are discussed in the House. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I would ask members from urban centres in Quebec and Ontario, areas that are highly industrialized and in which there is a high degree of mobility of employment, to rise and tell the government in no uncertain terms that the deduction of 3 per cent or a maximum of $150 is a mean, despicable, niggardly, unfair and inequitable provision. The least these hon. members can do is persuade the government that the minimum deductible amount, backed up by receipts, should be $500.
I am a man of reason, Mr. Chairman. I am a man who tries to be fair, a man of Irish background, a man of passion.
Now we understand you.

I am sure I have convinced you. I hope that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, a man who the other night said he represented Liberal-Labour-whatever that means-will express his views regarding this despicable provision that the government is attempting to present to the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder how the government arrived at this ceiling of $150 for deductible employment expenses. They must have pulled it out of the air because it bears no relationship to the real expenses incurred by working men in the course of their employment.
I should like to deal with the question of the automobile. Anyone who has operated a car knows it is almost impossible to keep it running for less than $500 a year. It may be argued that workers are running cars for their own convenience, that they run them for pleasure rather than to get to work. In my experience this is not the case. Virtual-
Income Tax Act
ly every working man I know has been forced to buy a car to keep his employment. Even in an area like Waterloo, where work and residence are closely related, it is almost impossible for a man to hold a job unless he has a car.
Very often workers can arrange car pools and can be picked up by fellow workers, but just as often that is not possible. Many people have called me because they have been disqualified for unemployment insurance after the breakdown of a car pool or because a fellow employee could no longer pick them up. The ruling was based on the fact that lack of transportation is no excuse. The Unemployment Insurance Commission recognizes the responsibility of a worker to provide his own transportation to the job site, yet the government does not recognize this responsibility under the Income Tax Act.
No one can provide transportation for $150 per year. When I suggested $500 I had that figure in mind as an absolute minimum. If you calculate the cost of insurance, licence plates, depreciation and the cost of gas and oil it would amount to at least $500. If you do not include depreciation, then the other costs plus the cost of repairs would amount to $500 per year. I suggest the ceiling should be $500 rather than $150 as proposed in this bill.
There was a time when the steel mills and the houses in which the workers lived were close together. An employee could run across the back yard, across the street or four of five blocks to get to work. People could manage in those days without a car, but now there is hardly anywhere in Canada which has zoning by-laws where this is the case. Residences and plants are separated by a considerable distance and municipal by-laws virtually ensure this, yet the income tax system does not make any allowance for this situation.
The purchase of a car is one of the things that faces young people starting out in marriage and working careers. I do not think there is a member of this House who has not received a telephone call from someone who is having difficulty meeting car payments. This is one of the main things which upsets the budgets of young people. I am sure other members have taken a look at these budgets and suggested to the individuals that they could not afford a car. I am sure hon. members have advised them to make other arrangements for transportation. These people invariably say they must have a car to get to work, that if it was only for pleasure they would give it up but they cannot find employment without a car.
I am sure many hon. members have received calls from time to time from constituents who have had their operator's licence taken away and have wound up on relief because they could not get to the job. If you cannot drive in modern society you virtually cannot work in most areas of this country. There are exceptions, but generally speaking a car has become a vital necessity for the workingman.
I am not one of those who is hung up on the idea that every person should have a car, and I am sure other hon. members share that view. There is a great need for public transportation. We must have a close look at zoning bylaws and the artificial, antiseptic transportation systems we now have. We must consider carefully the development of industrial and residential areas. We do not have

good public transportation at this time. Many workers in this country find public transportation inadequate. Perhaps this is because we do not have proper zoning bylaws. In any event, it is a fact of life that most workers must have automobiles, yet they are not allowed to deduct what is a necessary cost of employment. It is beyond my understanding why the government has not taken this fact into consideration. I am only referring to the cost of operating a car; I am not dealing with the cost of tools a workman requires or the cost of books required by a university professor in the course of his employment, although these are important items of expense.
I am not dealing with the safety equipment required by law and the many other expenses workingmen encounter in the continuation of employment. I am dealing with only this item to demonstrate how unrealistic is the $150 ceiling. The very least the government could do is make the allocation of car expenses as between pleasure and business, now available to self-employed persons or proprietors, available to the workingman. The workingman would be willing to prove the extent to which he needs his car for business as compared with pleasure. That is the kind of proof required of the self-employed and proprietors. The workingman is quite willing to provide the same kind of proof and accept the same kind of allocation of cost as between business and pleasure. But he is not given this opportunity. He is being fobbed off with this $150 which really should have been part of the original exemption. It has been put into this bill because the government knows the present tax system is inequitable but is not prepared to make significant changes.
The government is hoping that this little carrot or piece of camouflage will offset the discontent which exists in respect of the unfairness of the system. I cannot understand why a better system was not formulated. The parliamentary secretary has been helpful in answering our questions but I should like him to explain the basis upon which the government decided on the $150 ceiling. Is that all the government felt it could afford? Why has the government not been as arbitrary with the self-employed? Does the government feel $150 represents a realistic cost of finding and maintaining employment? I should like to hear about that and I ask the parliamentary secretary to try to justify the $150 in relation to the cost of operating an automobile.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak for a few minutes on a matter raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, namely, the problem faced by employees working on construction sites away from home. This matter was drawn to the attention of the government and members of the House of Commons by members and officials of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Employees Association.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw expressed the case very well when he pointed out the problem that exists in respect of discrimination between workers of the same construction crew, based solely on the particular type of project, whether it was classified as new construction or as repair work. I was very pleased to hear what the parliamentary secretary said in response to the hon. member's point in this regard and I am glad this provision is included in the bill. There is only one matter that requires clarification and I put it to the parliamentary secretary.
[Mr. Saltsman.J
In his response the parliamentary secretary made reference to the problem faced by contractors and employees of contractors. I recognize that this would be the case with contractors and their employees working at a site some distance from home, but I inquire about the situation in respect of the specific example raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, that is, involving the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Employees Association. This is not a case involving a contractor; it involves employees working directly for the Wheat Pool on construction and repair work. I want to obtain the assurance of the parliamentary secretary that the new provisions will apply to employees faced with that sort of situation just as they will apply to employees of a contractor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
My reference to contractors was not meant to mislead; it was merely an example. It is an employer-employee relationship that counts here, not the particular function that the employer or employee happens to be performing.
While I am on my feet, in response to the hon. member for Waterloo I would say that the $150 figure that was chosen as the ceiling was not designed to cover travelling expenses to and from work. Presidents of banks do not get their travelling expenses to and from work. This is not one of the expenses that is allowed any employee, any executive or anyone else. This is something that is simply not allowed. The $150 was not designed to cover that type of expense. It was designed to cover the special tools, the special clothing, and so on, that taxpayers need to earn their living. I can think of examples where $150 is not adequate and I can think of other examples where $150 will be more than adequate for the type of expenses which it was designed to cover.
It is simply not the purpose of this provision to cover all the expenses that a taxpayer incurs from the time he leaves his door after breakfast until he returns at supper time. In this context I submit that on a gross basis, on an average basis, the $150 is not a niggardly figure as has been suggested by hon. members opposite.

May I ask the parliamentary secretary a question? What does he think about travel expenses that are involved by a worker travelling from home to his place of work, especially when it is a considerable distance away, say 20 or 25 miles? Does he think that these expenses should be allowed, and what would the exemption be-because the hon. member for Waterloo said that the amount of $500 is a bare minimum in so far as expenses that a worker incurs in travelling from his home to his place of work are concerned. Would the parliamentary secretary please enlighten me with regard to his attitude concerning exemptions for expenses that workers incur in such instances?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do think that there are some expenses that are personal. The government makes no attempt to dictate to people where they should live in relation to their place of work. Personally, I see nothing intellectually or logically wrong with the idea that a taxpayer has the responsibility of delivering himself to work in the morning. This applies as well to the manager of an insurance company who is driving 20 miles in from the suburbs or

country estate to his office in downtown Toronto as it does to a worker in a steel plant in Hamilton who may be driving across town.
Perhaps we are fortunate that the economic system under which Canada has lived has permitted workers to move out from under the shadow of the steel mills and the smokestacks under which they lived. This is one of the benefits that Canadians have experienced as a result of our social and economic system. In making the decision to move away from the mill or the factory they have obviously decided to incur some expense and some inconvenience in getting to work, but obviously the price is worth paying because that is the decision they have made.
Hear, hear!

With reference to the matter raised by the hon. member for Waterloo, transportation allowances, I think that this does have some bearing. Many people in southern Ontario, where I live, are forced, due to lack of housing in our urban centres, to live in substandard housing and on abandoned farm lots. I know of many instances where workers on hourly rates drive 25 or 30 miles in broken-down automobiles in order to get to their work because the cost of housing in urban centres is so high that there is no way in which they can afford to live there.
After all is said and done, when you drive a round trip of 50 miles per day 300 days in the year, you put 15,000 miles on your automobile. This is done not out of choice but out of necessity. If those people were treated anything like the civil servants and allowed 16 cents a mile, they would probably be able to drive much better cars than they do at present. Although I do not normally agree with members of the party to my left, in this instance I feel that there should be some provision for the workers in this country who through no choice of their own are forced to live a long way from their work.

Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, although I have scrutinized the voluminous bill before us, I have found no provision likely to help Canadian workers employed in U.S. territory.
Earlier, I heard the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) seemingly boasting about the economic situation in Canada, claiming that people were able to travel wherever they wanted. I should however like to point out to him that the Canadian workers who have to cross the border in order to find jobs they cannot find in Canada, whose economic conditions have just been flaunted, must drive 40, 50 or 60 miles twice a week to reach logging camps. They cannot remain there during the weekend because the camps then close down for two days. Nevertheless, they are allowed no deduction for travel expenses. In fact, the famous bill containing over 700 pages completely ignores them. Yet, those workers have to file three income tax reports to satisfy the taxing authorities and the country in which they live. The first one is for the Canadian government, the second for the province of Quebec and the third for the American taxing authorities. And we are told that economic conditions are normal and satisfactory. Those who have drafted this bill, with the help of numerous civil servants who have been dealing with taxes for 20 or 25 years, have forgotten this category of workers.
I draw this fact to the attention of the parliamentary secretary and I would like to hear his views on this problem.

Mr. Chairman, I want to pursue the argument which the parliamentary secretary used to try to explain why the government feels the $150 expense allowance for workers is sufficient. If I understood him correctly, he said that the economic situation is such that the miner can afford to move more than a quarter of a mile away from the mine shaft, that he can afford to move 10, 15 or 20 miles away from his place of work and that the state does not and should not subsidize his expenses in travelling to and from work. But the parliamentary secretary did not address himself to the question that we have been asking. Why does the government have two standards? Why does the government apply that particular standard to the workingman, the factory worker, the man working in a mine or a mill?
To the doctor who lives in Rockcliffe and has an office in downtown Ottawa, who uses his car to go from his home to his office and from his office downtown to the Civic Hospital to see his patients, the government does not say, "You want to live in Rockcliffe and if you have to see your patients at the hospital you will have to pay expenses you incur." On the contrary, the government says to him, "You can charge off a very substantial part of the cost of your car, not just the gas and oil but depreciation and everything else."
The government says to the lawyer who wants to live in Kanata, uses his car to come to his office on Sparks Street or on Metcalfe Street and then uses it to go to the court

Mr. Chairman, I should like some clarification on the point that the parliamentary secretary raised a minute or two ago. I agree that if the parliamentary secretary takes his car and drives to the office or goes home, he is covered by other allowances. I think it is safe to say that unless he has an interest in the oil business or has another job, he is not going to get any money for his automobile. However, I think he would be hard pressed to pass on that example to professional people.
It may be true, and I think it is, that the doctor would not say that he had three patients in the Civic Hospital and was driving there from Rockcliffe, but I am sure that everyone here knows that the doctor can claim a percentage of the capital cost of his car, that he can claim a certain percentage of the operating expenses and as long as he does not claim 100 per cent the income tax department will not be very strict. This applied in the horse and buggy days as well. I presume when I was born the doctor had to drive 11 or 12 miles with the horse and buggy, but there was an allowance for it.
You are not that old.

I think the parliamentary secretary is not being fair to members of this House when he says he will not accept that there is a difference between the worker who takes his automobile to work, whether it be ten or 50 miles and where there is no other means of transportation, and the doctor who is driving his car in the course of his duties. In one case the worker can get no consideration for his car expenses against the income he earns, and in the other the doctor gets a percentage of the cost. I have operated on an expense account where I was supplied with a car. As long as I did not claim 100 per cent there was no difficulty. I owned two cars, so I said that I was using the company car for business and I allowed 5 per cent for casual driving. I used the other car for other purposes, so I was not entitled to that consideration.
I think the parliamentary secretary is being unfair to members who believe that the same type of concession should be given to the worker as is given to the professional man and self-employed citizens in respect of the operation of an automobile.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, since it is so close to ten o'clock I must apologize to the other hon. member who sought the floor. However, in view of the allegations which have been made I felt I should respond immediately rather than tomorrow. The fact is that the doctor in Rockcliffe does not have the right to claim the cost of motoring from home to the office against his income. The Department of National Revenue applies percentages of expenses and this varies with the experience of individuals. A doctor in a small rural community might very well be allowed over 75 per cent of the cost of his motor vehicle because it is regarded as a proper business expense.
What about the worker?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The doctor in the large community may be allowed as little as 50 per cent. I would not go so far as to say that each individual case is individually assessed, but certainly all are looked at in typical areas and if any professional man feels that he is using his vehicles for business purposes to an extent greater than the norm in
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
the community, he could justify this to the Department of National Revenue.
What about the worker driving to work? He is not going to get his expenses for operating that motor vehicle to and from work and he is not going to get any allowance while it is sitting in the parking lot outside the factory, either. The doctor drives the car in the course of earning his income. That is the criteria; the car is operated while the man is earning income-it is part of his necessary operations in earning his taxable income. It is not necessary for anybody to park a car next to his office building all day long.

The doctor does not take the car into the surgery, either.
Progress reported.

GRAIN-LIFT PROGRAM-REQUESTS TO FARMERS FOR REPAYMENTS-POSSIBILITY OF PROSECUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 14 1 asked the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) a question to which he did not give a satisfactory answer. My question was:
Is it the intention of the hon. gentleman's department to proceed with prosecutions in cases where aerial photographs have proved that a farmer's application in connection with the LIFT program was incorrect?
The minister gave an unsatisfactory answer to my question, more or less saying he would need more information. My supplementary question, which went unanswered, was:
Is it true that the PFRA Regina office is making demands with regard to these repayments?
I think that this has gone a little too far and it is time the farmer had some idea where he stands. Regarding the Lift program, the government was advised by all agriculturalists and members of parliament who were involved in farming that the Lift program was unsatisfactory. Farmers were forced into the Lift program against their will because if they did not participate they would no longer have a permit book, which is necessary if they are to sell grain.
Now very misleading figures have come out. The government anticipated that approximately $140 million would be paid into the lagging western economy in connection with agriculture but wound up paying less than $80 million, with approximately $2 million going into administration and aerial surveillance. This figure would have been increased greatly had it not been for the fact that the administration people took over the PFAA office that had been established and set up with personnel. If it

October 28, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
had not been for this, the cost of administration would have greatly exceeded $2 million.
The farmers were forced into the plan. I have heard of much dissatisfaction from people who did not receive any payment at all but had planned their crop year so as to receive some benefit from the program as well as from people who received the interim payment and later had a demand to pay it back. I cannot for the life of me see how the government hopes in any manner, shape or form to demand a repayment of those funds which were, in effect, a grant. One would not look for this kind of action from a former dean of law. It is ridiculous for the government to be asking for money back, because they have no legal right to it. In a number of cases that I took up with the department it was found that their figures were wrong and they made a further payment.
I should like to put on record the contents of one of several letters I have received. I received one letter from a young farmer. Part of it says that one year ago he applied for a payment under Operation Lift and in good faith accepted a payment of $135. This was accompanied by a letter saying that this was an initial payment and that the balance would be forwarded later. Upon receiving this initial payment he spent the money, later paid income tax on it and now they are requesting that he pay it back. That is one of several letters I have received.
May I also draw the minister's attention to the Western Producer, a farm paper, dated October 7, 1971. The heading over one letter reads, "Another Lift victim". Another letter to the editor is headed, "Lift cheque received, return demanded". That is the kind of thing you see in the press.
I am just wondering what this government thinks it can do. The farmers were forced into the program. I have heard many complaints from farmers who seeded land to forage. They were promised $4 per acre if they left it in grass and they were to receive $4 the following year if the inspector found that the land had been left as grassland. Now farmers are finding that these payments are being denied them. They have not received any payment on their forage. I am wondering what kind of deal the government is giving the farmers of western Canada when it engages in monkey business such as this. It is paying out money and then demanding it back. The government has displayed a great mistrust of the farmers by spending a great deal of money on aerial surveys, money which would have been much better paid to the producer who is in great need.
Is it morally or legally right for the government to make a payment with one hand and then demand it back with the other? I am sorry the minister is not in his place. I would like him to straighten out this mess in western Canada. Many farmers have received no payment whatsoever. In fact, their applications have not even been acknowledged. Many did not feel it was necessary to apply because they were not concerned with it. They later found they had to apply or they would not receive a permit book to sell grain. It is time the farmers of western Canada knew where the minister is going with his cockeyed Lift program.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Lessard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: GRAIN-LIFT PROGRAM-REQUESTS TO FARMERS FOR REPAYMENTS-POSSIBILITY OF PROSECUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the minister
[Mr. Cadieu.J
responsible for the Wheat Board and the application of the Lift program I am pleased to give the answer to the question asked by the hon. member. It is as follows. The Lift office at Regina-PFAA-has written to a number of farmers who for various reasons had received an overpayment under the Lift program. As the hon. member knows, in order to give farmers money quickly interim payments were made upon receipt of applications, with final balancing and a final payment made later. Aerial photographs were one of the means used for checking applications. Whether or not prosecutions will be undertaken in individual cases if repayments are not made voluntarily will be determined at a later time and will depend upon the circumstances of the particular case.

OIL-PROPOSED TAKE-OVER OF SUPERTEST BY BRITISH PETROLEUM-POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT ACTION-ACQUISITION BY PANARCTIC OILS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, October 26, as recorded at page 9032 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), who is also Acting Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the following question:
-is the government planning any measures to deal with the proposed take-over of the last major Canadian-owned distributor of petroleum products, Supertest, by British Petroleum Limited?
The minister's answer, to my way of thinking, was entirely unsatisfactory. He said:
Mr. Speaker, this situation has been under study and an announcement will be made in due course by the minister or somebody speaking for him.
I do not think the House should be asked to wait for this unidentified minister or person who is going to make a statement. The meeting of the shareholders is scheduled for November 2. The government ought to make a clear-cut statement as to what it intends to do about this proposed take-over. The point I want to make is that the oil industry is by far one of the wealthiest industries in Canada. In the Canadian Petroleum magazine issue of May, 1970, Mr. Carl O. Nickle, a former member of this House and the publisher of the Daily Oil Bulletin in Calgary, said that the value of reserves at present prices for oil, gas and sulphur is $1,118 billion. That is based on present oil, gas and sulphur prices. It is the equivalent of $50,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada.
This vast reservoir of wealth has been steadily slipping out of control of Canadians with the result that today over 80 per cent of oil and gas production is in the hands of foreign corporations. The major portion of the oil distribution facilities is in the hands of foreign corporations and 99 per cent of refining of petroleum products is in the hands of foreign investment.
There was some hope raised in people's minds when a few months ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) intervened to prevent the takeover of Home Oil Company, the last Canadian-owned company which had any hope of becoming a major oil producer. I give the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources full marks for the courage and vision he showed on that occasion. But, Mr. Speaker, oil production
October 28, 1971

must be accompanied by facilities for oil distribution, and Supertest is the last of the Canadian petroleum distributors, with 1,200 outlets. It will now be purchased, if the shareholders agree, on November 2, by British Petroleum Limited which, by the way, is 51 per cent owned by the government of Great Britain. If that happens we shall have virtually lost control, as far as Canadian companies are concerned, over the distribution of petroleum products in Canada.
The bright spot in the picture is that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and his predecessor showed considerable vision by investing public funds in Panarctic Oil, largely because many of the foreign investors who were quite willing to put money into Canada were not prepared to take the risk in the Arctic. The investment has paid off. Panarctic has discovered one of the largest deposits of natural gas in the world. The government's investment of between $30 million and $40 million is now worth $150 million to $200 million. Mr. Heatherington, president of Panarctic, has envisaged his company becoming a wholly integrated oil and gas concern. If this is so, it will need petroleum outlets.
This is why it is important that Supertest should not be allowed to pass into the hands of a foreign company. If Panarctic is not ready to act now, there is no reason why the Canada Development Corporation, providing the shareholders are intent on selling it, should not acquire Supertest and operate it until such time as Panarctic is in a position to need a distributor of petroleum products.
This is Canada's last chance to get a piece of the action. It is our last chance to prevent control of the wealthiest industry in our nation slipping entirely out of our hands. It is not enough for the minister to tell me that somebody is going to make an announcement. In the course of the next few days a decision will be made, a British company will take over an oil distributing firm and we shall find ourselves in the position of having lost almost the entire oil distribution network of this country to foreign companies.
I say to the government that if they want to retain the confidence of the Canadian public they must act now, otherwise the action they took with respect to Home Oil and Dennison Mines will have lost its effectiveness and we shall have allowed a valuable part of our economy to slip out of the hands of the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Allen B. Sulatycky (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy. Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: OIL-PROPOSED TAKE-OVER OF SUPERTEST BY BRITISH PETROLEUM-POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT ACTION-ACQUISITION BY PANARCTIC OILS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps in the next couple of minutes I shall be able to relieve the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) of some of his anxiety about this matter.
Following a joint statement by BP Canada Limited and Supertest Petroleum Corporation Limited on July 29, 1971, relative to a planned merger of interests between these two companies the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) wrote to confirm the prior notice given to the government of Canada by these two companies and to advise of the desire of the government to review the transaction in terms of the national interest, in accordance with the government's policy of understanding important economic activity taking place within
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Canada or affecting Canada. Subsequently, both meetings with senior officials of BP Canada and Supertest and the study of relevant material on the proposed takeover merger were undertaken but a final report to the government of Canada by officials was not made until Supertest issued its information circular dated October 7, 1971.
The government of Canada today has advised BP Canada Limited and Supertest Petroleum Corporation Limited that it does not intend to intervene. However, both BP Canada Limited and Supertest Petroleum Corporation Limited have been advised of the importance attached to maintaining a fully competitive market and their assurance that the merger is likely to enhance this fair competition in the interest of the consumer is relied upon.
Also taken into account is the assurance from these companies that western Canada produced oil will continue to be utilized in the Supertest marketing system, and that the merger of the BP and Supertest marketing interests will lead to the early consideration of expanded refinery capacity for the Ontario market, in accordance with the national oil policy.
